items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to use a scientific or graphing calculator to approximate definite integrals of functions.

Content:
This lesson is designed to help prepare you for the parts of the AP Calculus exam where graphing calculators are needed.

Content:
If you want to succeed on the AP Calculus exam, then you must acquire a physical graphing calculator and use it when completing this lesson.

Content:
Do not use any other type of online tool, as you will not be allowed to use it during the exam. You need to practice with the specific calculator that you will use on the AP exam so that you can solve problems quickly without wasting any time troubleshooting your calculator.

Content:
A comprehensive list of calculators that are permitted in the AP Calculus exams can be found here.

Content:
Throughout this lesson, we will list buttons that feature on a TI-84 Plus CE-T graphing calculator. We'll also mention some common alternative buttons on other calculator models.

Content:
Similar models will have the same or similar buttons, and even dissimilar models may have similar buttons.

Content:
If you have a different calculator model and cannot find the right buttons to press, the best way to resolve this is to either to

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (a) consult your calculator's manual, or

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (b) search online for a video that explains how to operate your calculator.

Content:
The best way to get familiar with your calculator is to consult its manual. Manuals can usually be found online. For example, a link to the manual for a TI-84 Plus CE-T can be found by entering the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] online manual TI-84 Plus CE-T

Content:
If you have a different model calculator, replace "TI-84 Plus CE-T" in the query above with your calculator's model.

Content:
Answers to common questions can be found by searching for online videos explaining how the calculator works. For example, to find a video that shows how to calculate an integral on a TI-84, you might type the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] video compute integral on a TI-84 calculator

Content:
Again, replace "TI-84" in the query above with your calculator's model. Also, bear in mind that videos for similar models might also help.

Content:
Watch Out! Some scientific calculators are not capable of approximating integrals! Check your calculator's manual to be sure.

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x),] defined as

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=2x + \sqrt{\cos x}.]

Content:
A sketch of this function is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/784c920a5556df001a586e94bf52da8c]

Content:
The finite area [MATH: \mathcal A] bounded by [MATH: f(x)] and the [MATH: x]-axes over the interval [MATH: x\in [a,0]] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{A} = \int_{a}^{0} 2x + \sqrt{\cos x} \: \textrm{d}x]

Content:
where [MATH: a] is the root of [MATH: f(x)] that's shown in the diagram.

Content:
To compute this integral numerically, we must first find an approximation for [MATH: a.] We can do this using our graphing calculator's root-finding functionality.

Content:
Following the usual procedure for approximating roots, we find that the lower limit (rounded to three decimal places) is

Content:
[MATH: a \approx -0.472.]

Content:
So, the area [MATH: \mathcal A] is approximately equal to

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-0.472}^{0} 2x + \sqrt{\cos x} \: \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
Finally, evaluating this integral using our graphing calculator in the usual way, we get

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-0.472}^{0} 2x+\sqrt{\cos x} \, \textrm{d}x \approx 0.240]

Content:
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to use a scientific or graphing calculator to approximate definite integrals of functions.

Content:
This lesson is designed to help prepare you for the parts of the AP Calculus exam where graphing calculators are needed.

Content:
If you want to succeed on the AP Calculus exam, then you must acquire a physical graphing calculator and use it when completing this lesson.

Content:
Do not use any other type of online tool, as you will not be allowed to use it during the exam. You need to practice with the specific calculator that you will use on the AP exam so that you can solve problems quickly without wasting any time troubleshooting your calculator.

Content:
A comprehensive list of calculators that are permitted in the AP Calculus exams can be found here.

Content:
Throughout this lesson, we will list buttons that feature on a TI-84 Plus CE-T graphing calculator. We'll also mention some common alternative buttons on other calculator models.

Content:
Similar models will have the same or similar buttons, and even dissimilar models may have similar buttons.

Content:
If you have a different calculator model and cannot find the right buttons to press, the best way to resolve this is to either to

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (a) consult your calculator's manual, or

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (b) search online for a video that explains how to operate your calculator.

Content:
The best way to get familiar with your calculator is to consult its manual. Manuals can usually be found online. For example, a link to the manual for a TI-84 Plus CE-T can be found by entering the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] online manual TI-84 Plus CE-T

Content:
If you have a different model calculator, replace "TI-84 Plus CE-T" in the query above with your calculator's model.

Content:
Answers to common questions can be found by searching for online videos explaining how the calculator works. For example, to find a video that shows how to calculate an integral on a TI-84, you might type the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] video compute integral on a TI-84 calculator

Content:
Again, replace "TI-84" in the query above with your calculator's model. Also, bear in mind that videos for similar models might also help.

Content:
Watch Out! Some scientific calculators are not capable of approximating integrals! Check your calculator's manual to be sure.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Calculating an Integral

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x),] defined as

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=\sqrt{\sin x}.]

Content:
A sketch of this function is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/37225afd53ce6b7458319f9431ed3c7f]

Content:
The finite area [MATH: \mathcal A] bounded by [MATH: f(x)] and the [MATH: x]-axis over the interval [MATH: x\in [0,\pi]] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{A} = \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin x} \: \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
Let's use our graphing calculator to approximate this area. Since the function we want to integrate contains trigonometric functions, your calculator must be in radians mode!

Content:
We bring up the definite integral option on most calculators in one of the following ways:

Content:
1. Using the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\displaystyle\color{gray}\,\int_{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}^{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}} \bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{\big|0\big|}}\,}] button. You may need to press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,2\text{nd}\,}] (or [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{shift}\,}]) first.
2. Using the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{math}\,}] (or [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{calc}\,}]) button and selecting the "integration" option. Note that this might be called [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{fnInt}\,}] or similar.

Content:
The next steps depend on whether your calculator uses derivative or function notation. We'll discuss both. You're encouraged to read both instructions as there are several parallels.

Content:
Integral Notation

Content:
If your calculator uses derivative notation, you should see a prompt that looks similar to the following:

Content:
[MATH: \int_{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}^{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}} \bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{\big|0\big|}} \,\textrm{d}\,{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}]

Content:
In this case, we fill in the empty boxes as follows:

Content:
- Enter [MATH: 0] for the lower integration limit. Then, press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleright\,}] to move the cursor to the upper integration limit, and enter the value [MATH: \pi.]

The prompt should now look as follows:
[MATH: \int_{0}^{\pi} \bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{\big|0\big|}} \,\textrm{d}\,{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}]
- Navigate the cursor to the next empty box by pressing [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleright\,}.] Enter the function definition by pressing the following keys:
[MATH: \bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\sqrt{\phantom{0}}} \quad\:\:
\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\sin\,}\quad\:\:
\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}X,T,\theta,n} \quad\:\:
\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}]
The prompt should now look as follows:
[MATH: \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin(x)} \,\textrm{d}\,{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}]
- Navigate the cursor to the next empty box by pressing [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleright\,}.] Press [MATH: \bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}X,T,\theta,n}] to enter the variable that we're integrating with respect to.

The prompt should now look as follows:
[MATH: \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin(x)} \,\textrm{d}x]
- Finally, press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\textrm{enter}\,},] and the calculator will return the numerical value of the integral.

Content:
Following the above steps, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{\sin x} \: \textrm{d}x\approx 2.396]
rounded to three decimal places.

Content:
Function Notation

Content:
If your calculator uses function notation, then instead of being presented with

Content:
[MATH: \int_{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}^{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}} \bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{\big|0\big|}} \,\textrm{d}\,{\bbox[gray]{\,\phantom{0}}}]

Content:
you'll instead see a prompt that looks similar to the following:

Content:
[MATH: \text{integral}\Big(
\bbox[gray]{\color{white}\phantom{\Big|}\text{expression}\phantom{\Big|}},
\bbox[gray]{\color{white}\phantom{\Big|}\text{variable}\phantom{\Big|}},
\bbox[gray]{\color{white}\phantom{\Big|}\text{lowerBound}\phantom{\Big|}},
\bbox[gray]{\color{white}\phantom{\Big|}\text{upperBound}\phantom{\Big|}}\Big)]

Content:
In this case, we place the function definition in the first box, the variable in the second box, and the lower and upper limits in the third and fourth boxes, respectively.

Content:
